report.headline: Hello. I know how exhausting it can be when screen time ends in a loud meltdown, especially when you are trying your best to manage it while juggling other things. It is incredibly stressful to hear your child cry, but you are doing a great job trying to set boundaries. Let's look at how we can make these transitions smoother for both of you.

sections.title: What Went Well
sections.body:
You did a wonderful job giving a direct, specific command initially ("Hand it over, please").

Most importantly, even though Jd protested loudly, you held the boundary and did not give the phone back. Staying consistent when your child is upset is incredibly hard, but you stayed firm and didn't cave in!

sections.title: Emotion Timeline
sections.body:
*Pattern:* Jd started with mild verbal protests, which quickly escalated into stomping and loud crying once the phone was physically removed. The meltdown was sustained and prolonged because of the ongoing verbal back-and-forth, sibling interference, and lengthy explanations/negotiations. 

*Core focus for next session:* **Co-regulate first, then teach (and avoid nagging).** When Jd is highly emotional, his "thinking brain" (prefrontal cortex) is offline. Explaining rules, negotiating ("You have to be a good boy"), or using threats overstimulates him and actually fuels the meltdown. Next time, once the boundary is set and the phone is away, stop explaining. Offer calm, quiet support by naming his feeling ("You are mad screen time is over"), staying close, and holding the limit without extra words.

sections.title: Other Best Practices
sections.body:
- Give simple countdown warnings
- Use a timer to make it neutral
- Redirect the child to a bridging activity and model it
